extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and communication researchers studying news production
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and organizational practices that determine what becomes news (newsworthiness), how events are typified (hard/soft/spot/developing/continuing), and how time/space/technology/staffing shape selection and processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment of newsworthiness is a negotiated phenomenon, constituted in the activities of a complex bureaucracy designed to oversee the news net.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness is not a fixed objective property of events but the outcome of editorial negotiation and organizational processes; editors 'create and recreate negotiated standards of judgment' through routine practices such as editorial conferences and assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional centralization and source status
rubrics_metrics.description: The news net excludes some occurrences because of a pattern of centralization at legitimated institutions and orders priorities by which sort of employee or service produced an item (reporter or stringer, staff or Associated Press reporter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source identity and institutional legitimacy influence selection and placement; items from central, legitimated institutions or from higher-status reporters are privileged in allocation and priority-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial anchoring of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurrences that may qualify as news events are expected to occur at specific locations, and the rhythm of newswork is designed to catch those occurrences that happen at the appropriate place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations distribute reporters to central spatial locations (beats, bureaus) and routinize coverage according to geography; proximity and dispersion of reporters shape which occurrences are noticed and covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal anchoring and rhythms
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswork is synchronized with the temporal rhythms of institutions: reporters' arrival and departure times, deadlines, and planned schedules influence what can be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical newsroom schedules (e.g., reporters arriving 10–11am, leaving 6–7pm; skeletal late-night staff) make coverage of events outside those hours difficult, so timing determines whether an occurrence will be considered newsworthy or practical to cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / 'quickening' (speed of dissemination)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quickening ... is the essence of news' — if newsworkers do not act quickly, hard-news stories become obsolete before dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed is a core evaluative dimension: stories that cannot be gathered, edited, and disseminated within the required timetable risk being dropped or downgraded; timeliness varies by story type (hard news vs soft features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard versus soft news
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news concerns occurrences potentially available to analysis or interpretation and 'factual presentations'; soft news (features/human-interest) deals with the texture of human life and need not be as timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard-news items typically include accidents, crimes, official messages and require prompt coverage; soft-news items (features on human interest) can be scheduled, prepared in advance, and placed in slower outlets (e.g., Sunday papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot news
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot news is unscheduled, sudden, unforeseen events (fires, robberies, accidents) that must be processed quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot news requires rapid mobilization of resources; newsrooms create 24-hour arrangements and reserve staff to anticipate such events while balancing cost and existing assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing news
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing news is a subclass of hard news characterized by facts still emerging — stories that remain 'developing' so long as information is still being gathered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing stories demand ongoing information gathering and repeated updates; they often occupy resources over an extended period until facts stabilize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing news
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing news comprises a series of stories on the same subject over time (e.g., legislative bills, trials, campaigns); such content tends to occur over an extended period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing items are managed through planned coverage and prediction of event trajectories; they justify assigning reporters for prolonged attention and allow for serial reporting strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling types: nonscheduled, prescheduled, unscheduled
rubrics_metrics.description: Events-as-news are classified as nonscheduled (timing determined by newsworkers), prescheduled (announced for a future date by convenors), or unscheduled (occur unexpectedly), and this affects when and how they are processed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most hard-news stories are prescheduled or unscheduled; nonscheduled stories (investigations) allow newsrooms to control timing of dissemination; knowledge of scheduling type guides staff allocation and editorial planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff availability and resource allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and timing of available reporters constrain coverage — few reporters are available before 10am or after 7pm, reserve reporters are held for emergencies, and late assignments reduce capacity for major stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment decisions must weigh opportunity costs: sending a reserve reporter to an evening occurrence may deplete capacity for a larger breaking story; roster management and shift planning are key evaluative levers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and processing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Different news technologies have distinct time rhythms (film vs videotape vs print); processing requirements (developing film, editing) influence what can be covered in time for deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological limits determine feasible coverage: television film must be processed to meet telecast times; electronic/live capabilities modify constraints; technology affects typification and resource choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity, competition, and need for special competitive merits
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations face a 'glut of occurrences' and must winnow many potential stories; late or marginal occurrences must present 'special competitive merits' to be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors allocate limited column/in-airtime against many claims; stories compete on perceived importance, uniqueness, and timeliness, and wire-service or desk editors may fill remaining space using budget and priority rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning across days / projecting work
rubrics_metrics.description: News media plan across days (e.g., memos about upcoming trials) to allocate staff for lengthy coverage and to avoid degrading routine beat reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance projection allows assignment of reporters to long events (trial coverage), freeing others for daily beats; planning decisions influence which occurrences will be covered and at what depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typifications as relatively content-free practical categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Typifications (hard/soft/spot/developing/continuing) are relatively content-free in that they classify events by how they happen (timing, predictability, resource demands) rather than strictly by substantive content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practical categories are embedded in newsworkers' routines and are used to routinize processing, predict resource needs, and make rapid decisions under organizational constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source timing and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: News promoters and officials may manipulate timing and setting (e.g., emergency news conferences shortly before deadlines, lack of telephones) to constrain reporters' ability to check claims and to influence coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters must be aware of—and sometimes resist—source strategies intended to exploit newsroom rhythms; manipulative scheduling can reduce verification time and skew selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter status, beat assignment, and availability effects
rubrics_metrics.description: High-status reporters or those assigned to lengthy projects are less available for immediate coverage; reporters interpret tasks as 'filing a daily story' and allocation influences both quantity and depth of output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status and preassignment affect which reporters are available for breaking stories; editors balance prestige/skill assignments against the need for daily output and coverage breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire service influence and editorial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services and wire-service editors shape coverage (e.g., offering slightly more national than international news); late-hour selection by wire editors fills columns using service budgets and remaining space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence on wire copy and wire-editor choices introduces systematic biases (topic skew, national emphasis) and becomes part of the negotiated process of what reaches readers/viewers.
